::: {.lead}
*Pocket Pets* is a mobile game made by a small studio. After version 2.0,
many players write to the support team. One player asks why only one core
of the phone is busy. Another player cannot download the new island. A third
player pressed a button in the settings and lost all the pets. A fourth
player asks why the new island loads so slowly. Each question
is about one of three parts of the device: the **processor (CPU)**, the
**memory (RAM)** or the **storage**. In lecture 1 you met these parts. In this
lesson you look inside them and learn what each part does in a game. Every
section ends with a short task. You do it on the lab computer, on your phone
or in a simulator.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary cpu cpu-core clock-rate thread memory-hierarchy cache memory byte app-package process loading storage ssd app-storage >}}

## 2.1 Why eight cores do not make a game eight times faster

Phone adverts often say "octa-core, 3 GHz". What do these two numbers mean
for a game?

A **core** is a small, complete processor inside the CPU. A core runs one
list of instructions at a time. This list is called a **thread**. A CPU with
eight cores ("octa-core") can run eight threads at the same time.

Most phone CPUs have two kinds of core (@fig-cores):

- **performance cores**: big and fast, but they use more battery;
- **efficiency cores**: small and slower, but they save battery.

The **clock rate** tells how fast one core works. It is measured in
gigahertz (GHz): 3 GHz means 3 billion clock ticks per second.

![A phone CPU with two performance cores and six efficiency cores. The operating system puts each thread of the game on a core.](images/cpu-cores.png){#fig-cores width=94%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Core and thread"}
A **core** is a processing unit inside the CPU. It runs one list of
instructions at a time. A **thread** is one such list inside a program. The
operating system decides which thread runs on which core.
:::

A game has one **main thread**. In every frame, it runs the game logic in a
fixed order: read the input, move the characters, check collisions, update
the score. Each step needs the result of the step before it, so only one core
can do this work. Other work, such as physics, loading and sound, runs on
**worker threads**. Worker threads can use the other cores.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — Splitting one frame across cores"}
On one core, a frame needs 16 ms: 10 ms of game logic on the main thread, and
6 ms of physics that can be shared equally among cores.

1. One core: $10 + 6 = 16$ ms.
2. Two cores share the 6 ms: $10 + 3 = 13$ ms.
3. Six cores share the 6 ms: $10 + 1 = 11$ ms.
4. Six cores make the frame faster, but not six times faster. The 10 ms of
   the main thread always stay on one core.
:::

![Time per frame in Example 2.1 with one, two and six cores. The main-thread part does not get shorter.](images/frame-split.png){#fig-split width=86%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Eight cores at 3 GHz make 24 GHz." This is wrong. Each core works on its
own thread, and the main thread of the game uses only one core.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch the cores at work"}
On a lab computer (Windows):

1. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open **Task Manager**. Choose
   **Performance → CPU**.
2. Right-click the graph. Choose **Change graph to → Logical processors**.
   You now see one small graph for each thread that the CPU can run at the
   same time.
3. Open the simulator of section 3.2 or a browser game. Watch the graphs for
   30 seconds.

*Your result:* the number of cores and of logical processors. Both numbers
are under the graphs. Add one sentence: is one graph very busy, or are all
graphs busy?

::: {.check}
A typical lab computer shows 4 to 8 cores (8 to 16 logical processors). While
the simulator runs, one graph is often much busier than the others: the main
thread of a program runs on one core at a time.
:::
:::

## 2.2 Why the processor keeps a small memory next to it

The CPU is very fast. Main memory (RAM) is much slower. When the CPU asks RAM
for a value, it waits about 100 nanoseconds (ns). In that time, one core
could do hundreds of steps. To wait less, a computer keeps data at different
levels. This is called the **memory hierarchy** (@fig-hierarchy).

![The memory hierarchy. Each level is bigger and slower than the level above it. The times are typical values.](images/memory-hierarchy.png){#fig-hierarchy width=92%}

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Memory hierarchy and cache"}
The **memory hierarchy** puts the memories of a computer in levels. Near the
core, memory is small and very fast. Far from the core, memory is big and
slow. The **cache** is a small, very fast memory next to the cores. It keeps
copies of data that the core used a short time ago.
:::

| Level | Typical size | Time to read one value | Keeps data without power? |
|---|---|---|---|
| cache | a few MB | about 1 ns | no |
| main memory (RAM) | 4–16 GB in a phone | about 100 ns | no |
| flash storage or SSD | 64 GB – 2 TB | about 100 µs (100 000 ns) | yes |
| hard disk | 1–20 TB | about 10 ms (10 000 000 ns) | yes |

: The levels of the memory hierarchy (typical values). {#tbl-hierarchy}

Why does the cache help so much? A game reads the same data again and again.
For example, in every frame, the movement code, the camera and the collision
check all read the player's position. After the first read, the position is in
the cache, and the next reads are fast.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — The hierarchy on a human scale"}
Imagine that one nanosecond lasts one second.

1. A read from the cache (1 ns) takes **1 second**: you look at your desk.
2. A read from RAM (100 ns) takes **100 seconds**: you walk to the next room.
3. A read from flash storage (100 000 ns) takes **100 000 seconds**, about
   **28 hours**: you travel to another city.
4. So the CPU wants the data it needs most in the cache, as close as
   possible.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/data-trip.html" poster="sims/data-trip.png" title="Data Trip: fetch data through the memory hierarchy" kind="sim" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Fetch the data yourself"}
Open the **Data Trip** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Fetch one value from the cache, from RAM and from flash storage.
2. Write the time and the human-scale time of each level in a table.

*Your result:* the table, and one sentence in your own words: what does the
cache do?

::: {.check}
Cache about 1 ns (1 second on the human scale), RAM about 100 ns (about 2
minutes), flash storage about 100 000 ns (about a day). The cache keeps
copies of data used a short time ago next to the core, so the core waits
less.
:::
:::

## 2.3 Why the game shows a loading screen

A mobile game comes as one file, an **app package**. It holds the game's code
and its **assets**: pictures, 3D models, sounds and levels. On Android, the
package that the phone downloads is called an APK. On iPhone, it is called
an IPA.

**Installing** copies the package into the phone's storage. The game does not
run yet: it uses storage, but no memory.

When the player taps the icon, the operating system **launches** the game
(@fig-launch):

1. it creates a **process**: a running program with its own part of memory;
2. it **loads** the game's code from storage into memory (RAM);
3. the game loads the assets of the first scene;
4. the game starts, and the first frame appears.

![Launching a game: the operating system creates a process and copies code and assets from storage into memory.](../week-01/images/launch.png){#fig-launch width=88%}

Why is there a loading screen? Because storage is much slower than memory.
Phone storage reads from about 100 MB per second in cheap phones to more than
1000 MB per second in expensive phones.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — Why loading is slower on a cheap phone"}
The first level of a game needs 1500 MB of assets. Phone A reads 1500 MB per
second. Phone B reads 150 MB per second.

1. Phone A: $1500 / 1500 = 1$ second.
2. Phone B: $1500 / 150 = 10$ seconds.
3. Same game, same level: ten times slower, only because of the storage
   speed.
:::

Memory is limited too. When the player switches to another app, the game
waits in the background. If memory gets full, the operating system closes
background games to free memory. This is why a game sometimes starts again
from its title screen when the player comes back. Good games save the
player's progress when they go to the background.

Main memory (RAM) holds everything that the game needs *now* (@fig-ram):

- the game's **code**;
- the **assets** of the current scene: **textures**, 3D models and sounds;
- the game **state**: positions, health and score, which change in every
  frame.

The operating system and the apps in the background use the same RAM. So the
game gets only a part of it.

![Main memory of a phone during play. The game's part holds code, textures, models, sound and state.](images/game-ram.png){#fig-ram width=92%}

We measure the size of data in **bytes**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.3 — The byte and its multiples"}
A **byte** is 8 bits. It can hold one number from 0 to 255, for example the
amount of red in one pixel. Each bigger unit is 1024 times the unit before
it: 1 KB (kilobyte) = 1024 bytes, 1 MB (megabyte) = 1024 KB,
1 GB (gigabyte) = 1024 MB, 1 TB (terabyte) = 1024 GB.
:::

Windows counts in this way, and this course does too. So
1 MB = 1024 × 1024 bytes.

Files and memory are measured in the same units. A game of 1.5 GB is
1.5 × 1024 = 1536 MB, and a 2 GB update is 2048 MB.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"A phone with more storage starts games faster." No: the *size* of storage
decides how many games fit. The *speed* of storage decides how fast they load.
The size of *memory* decides how much can stay loaded at once.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch the memory fill"}
On a lab computer:

1. Open Task Manager → **Processes**. Click the **Memory** column to sort the
   list.
2. Write down the memory that the browser uses.
3. Open five pages with many pictures (a photo gallery, a map, a video site).
   Wait ten seconds. Write down the browser's memory again.

*Your result:* the two numbers, and one sentence: what does the extra memory
hold?

::: {.check}
The browser's memory grows, for example from 400 MB to 900 MB. The extra
memory holds the open pages: their pictures, code and data.
:::
:::

## 2.4 Where the game lives when it is not running

When you switch the phone off, the game, its downloaded levels and your
progress must not be lost. They are kept in **storage**. Storage keeps its
data without power.

There are two kinds of storage (@fig-storage):

- A **hard disk drive (HDD)** stores data on spinning disks. An arm moves over
  the disks to read the data. It is cheap, but slow.
- A **solid-state drive (SSD)** stores data on flash memory chips. It has no
  moving parts and is much faster. Phones use the same flash chips, fixed on
  the phone's board. New game consoles use fast SSDs too.

![Kinds of storage (left) and the parts of an installed game in storage (right).](images/storage.png){#fig-storage width=94%}

A phone shows each game in storage as three parts.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.4 — App size, user data and cache"}
The **app size** is the installed game: its code and its built-in assets. The
**user data** is what the game creates for this player: saved progress,
settings and downloaded levels. The **cache** is a set of temporary files that
the game can download or create again. (This storage cache is not the
processor cache of section 3.2. The idea is the same: both keep copies to save
time.)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.4 — Pocket Pets in storage"}
On one phone, *Pocket Pets* uses: app 1.1 GB, downloaded islands 2.4 GB,
saved progress 2 MB, cache 300 MB (about 0.3 GB).

1. Total: $1.1 + 2.4 + 0.3$ = about 3.8 GB (the 2 MB of progress is very small).
2. **Clear cache** frees 300 MB. Nothing important is lost: the game creates
   the files again when it needs them.
3. **Clear storage** (Android) deletes the user data: the islands and the
   progress. If the game does not save the progress online, the pets are gone.
:::

A new laptop has a "1 TB" SSD, but Windows shows about 931 GB. No space is
missing. The maker of the drive counts in steps of 1000 (1 TB = 1000 GB), but
Windows counts in steps of 1024 (1 TB = 1024 GB). So the same space gives a
smaller number in Windows. On a phone, the "missing" space has
another reason: the operating system itself uses part of the storage.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Clear cache and Clear storage do the same thing." This is wrong. Clear cache
deletes temporary files. Clear storage deletes the player's data.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A game in your phone's storage"}
On your phone, open the storage screen of one game:

- **Android:** Settings → Apps → *(the game)* → Storage. You see App size,
  User data and Cache. (The names can be a little different on some phones.)
- **iPhone:** Settings → General → iPhone Storage → *(the game)*. You see
  App Size and Documents & Data.

Do **not** press Clear storage, Offload App or Delete App.

*Your result:* the size of each part, and one answer: which part would grow
if you downloaded a new level?

::: {.check}
A good answer lists the app size, the user data (documents and data) and
the cache, for example 1.1 GB, 2.4 GB and 0.3 GB. A new level makes the
user data grow, because downloaded levels are user data.
:::
:::

## Case study: the Pocket Pets support desk

*Pocket Pets* is a made-up mobile game. Version 2.0 adds a new island of
900 MB. In the first week, the support team receives five messages:

1. "My phone has eight cores, but only one is really busy."
2. "The island download needs 1.6 GB, and my phone has 1.2 GB free."
3. "I pressed Clear storage, and my pets are gone."
4. "My new 1 TB laptop SSD shows only 931 GB."
5. "My cheap phone reads 180 MB per second. The island takes long to load."

Each message is about one component and what it does. In the Game challenge
of the interactive page, you answer these players, and in the mini-game
below you sort ten such messages.

{{< sim file="sims/pocket-pets.html" poster="sims/pocket-pets.png" title="Pocket Pets: answer the support desk" kind="game" height="560" >}}

## Further reading

Tanenbaum and Austin, *Structured Computer Organization*, 6th ed., Chapter 2:
section 2.1 (processors), section 2.2 (primary memory and cache memory) and
section 2.3 (secondary memory: the memory hierarchy, magnetic disks and
solid-state disks).

## Exercises

1. What is the difference between a core and a thread?
2. A frame needs 12 ms on the main thread and 8 ms of work that can be shared
   equally among cores. What is the frame time with one core? With four
   cores?
3. Why does a phone have efficiency cores?
4. Put in order from fastest to slowest: RAM, cache, hard disk, flash storage.
5. The player's position is read many times in every frame. Why is the game
   faster when the position is in the cache?
6. What does installing a game fill, and what does launching it fill?
7. A level needs 600 MB. The phone reads 200 MB per second. How long does it
   load?
8. How many MB is a 3 GB update?
9. What does a player lose with Clear cache? And with Clear storage?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A core is a part of the CPU (hardware). A thread is a list of instructions in a program (software). The operating system puts each thread on a core.
2. One core: 12 + 8 = 20 ms. Four cores: 12 + 2 = 14 ms.
3. Efficiency cores do light work with little energy, so the battery lasts longer.
4. Cache, RAM, flash storage, hard disk.
5. The cache is next to the core and very fast (about 1 ns). After the first read, the core finds the position there and does not wait for RAM (about 100 ns).
6. Installing fills storage; launching loads the game into memory (RAM).
7. 600 ÷ 200 = 3 seconds.
8. 3 × 1024 = 3072 MB.
9. Clear cache: nothing important (temporary files). Clear storage: the user data (progress and downloaded levels).
:::
